title: The AI reviewer that is allowed to say yes
dek: PyTorch now lets an AI approve its maintainers' pull requests, rebuilding Meta's RADAR in the open with its guardrails written down. Plus a skill that phones home, Balatro's full wishlist curve, and Google Play's address rule.

theme.mood: a Saturday about who gets to approve, and what to check first

tldr.text: PyTorch's **GreenLight** lets an AI reviewer running Claude Code approve maintainers' pull requests. It copies Meta's RADAR, which has landed 331K+ low-risk changes.
Its guardrails are worth copying: approval tied to one commit, a revert bans the PR, and files like CLAUDE.md are stripped before the AI reads the change.
An open issue says Convex's agent skills send your app idea to a remote host and pipe scripts into bash. Read skills like dependencies.
Balatro's creator published every month of wishlists, 48 to 208,401, and what moved each step.
Google Play will show individual traders' phone and address from March 1, 2027. Declare by February 1.

blocks.title: PyTorch lets an AI reviewer approve pull requests, copying Meta's playbook
blocks.gist: PyTorch now runs an open-source bot that reviews pull requests from its maintainers with an AI and approves the ones it judges safe. It copies a system Meta uses internally, which has already landed more than 331,000 code changes.
blocks.background: Meta described its system, RADAR, in a paper in May. PyTorch, the machine learning framework Meta started, said then that it would rebuild it in the open.
body: **GreenLight** scans open pull requests every five minutes, sends eligible ones to an AI review that runs through **Claude Code**, and approves the ones that come back with a land verdict. Only authors already named in PyTorch's merge rules can get a real approval. Everyone else is reviewed in shadow: the verdict is recorded, but never acted on.

Meta's **RADAR** is the larger version. It sorts each change by where it came from (a person, a bot, an automated runbook), applies hard gates, scores its risk with a trained model, asks an LLM to confirm the change falls in safe categories such as dead code removal, tests or logging, and only then lands it, after a delay in which a person can still say no. Any failure sends the change to a human.

The reason is volume. Meta's paper says lines per human-landed change rose 105.9% in a year and changes per developer rose 51%, mostly from AI agents, while the share reviewed within a day fell. OpenAI told QCon San Francisco it aims to auto-approve at least 90% of routine pull requests on one product.

nodes.note: No open-source, audited or special-review code

diagram.caption: How Meta's RADAR decides which changes land without a reviewer, from the RADAR paper and InfoQ's summary. GreenLight is the open, narrower version.

stat.label: changes RADAR has landed at Meta, of 535K+ it reviewed

blocks.why: When agents write more code than people can read, the question becomes which changes may skip a human. This is the first open, working answer from a team at scale, with its guardrails written down.
blocks.forYou: Your routines already open PRs on your own repos; GreenLight's shadow mode is the safe way to test an auto-approver on them: let it vote for a few weeks, compare with what you actually merged, and only then let it approve the narrowest category (tests, docs).

terms.def: A proposed code change that waits for review before it is merged.
A large language model, the kind of AI behind chat assistants and coding agents.
Running a system for real but ignoring its decisions, so you can compare them with what people did.
A scripted, repeatable change, such as a dependency bump, that a bot applies across many files.

deep: RADAR's risk thresholds depend on the source: allowlisted runbooks may land up to the 50th percentile of risk, other bots up to the 20th, and human-authored changes only up to the 5th. Runbooks also need a 60-day record with zero production incidents and are capped at 2,000 changes a day. Open-source and SOX-scoped code is never eligible.

The paper reports a 60.31% approve rate after relaxing the threshold from the 25th to the 50th percentile, revert rates one third and production incident rates one fiftieth of non-RADAR changes, and a 35% shorter median review time. The authors call the safety comparison observational, not causal. The abstract also claims time to close fell by 'over 330%', which cannot be read literally.

GreenLight's README says the review runs through claude-code-action (CLI last verified at 2.1.169), with a 20-minute target and a 33-minute hard limit per review, and declines changes over about 2,000 lines or 200 files.

blocks.title: Five guardrails in GreenLight worth copying
blocks.gist: The open-source bot's README spells out how it avoids approving the wrong thing, and most of the rules work for any team, with or without AI.
blocks.intro: From the GreenLight README in PyTorch's test-infra repository.

items.title: Trusted authors only
items.text: Only people already allowed to approve code can get an AI approval. Everyone else is reviewed in shadow, recorded but never approved.

items.title: Approval belongs to one exact commit
items.text: The approval is tied to the commit the AI read. Push anything new and the merge gate waits for a fresh review.

items.title: One revert, banned for good
items.text: If a change it approved is reverted, the bot withdraws its approval and never reviews that pull request again, even if the label is removed.

items.title: Strip the contributor's instructions
items.text: Before the AI reads a pull request it deletes files such as CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and .cursorrules from it, so a contributor cannot slip instructions to the reviewer.

items.title: Say no to big changes
items.text: Anything over about 2,000 lines or 200 files gets an automatic no, with the reason 'scope too large'.

blocks.why: An AI reviewer reads text written by the person it is judging. Stripping their instruction files and pinning approval to one commit close the two easiest ways to game it.
blocks.forYou: Copy the instruction-file stripping into any routine that reviews code it did not write: run reviews on a checkout with CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules removed, and restore skills only from main.

terms.def: One saved snapshot of changes in a Git repository, with a unique id.
A file of standing instructions that Claude Code reads at the start of every session in a project.

blocks.title: An agent skill that sends your app idea away and pipes scripts into bash
blocks.gist: An open GitHub issue says Convex's official skills for coding agents quietly send the user's project idea to a remote server and run downloaded scripts, worded to slip past the agent's safety checks.
blocks.background: Skills are packaged instructions and scripts that a coding agent such as Claude Code loads to learn a task. Convex is a hosted backend for web apps.
blocks.intro: Claims from issue #64, opened October 26 and on the Hacker News front page on November 27. No maintainer has replied.

items.title: Your idea leaves the machine
items.text: The quickstart skill posts the user's one-line project idea to a convex.site host, labelled telemetry in a code comment, without telling the user.

items.title: Remote scripts run unseen
items.text: The add skill downloads scripts from the same host and pipes them straight into bash; a later comment adds unpinned dependencies.

items.title: Split to dodge the check
items.text: Another skill splits download and run into two calls, saying one combined command is the shape safety classifiers block.

items.title: What to look for
items.text: Before installing any skill, search it for outbound POSTs, curl piped to a shell, and instructions about avoiding the agent's checks.

blocks.why: A skill is code and prompt from someone else running with your agent's permissions. Read it like a dependency, because that is what it is.
blocks.forYou: Grep every third-party skill in your Claude Code setup for curl, POST and '| bash' before the next routine run; the Nov 25 server-skills hook (PreSkillShellCommand) can block the shell part.

terms.def: The command-line shell on most Linux and Mac machines; piping a download into it runs the file at once.
Data a program sends home about how it is used.

blocks.title: Cloudflare gives any site a search endpoint for agents
blocks.gist: One switch in Cloudflare's dashboard now indexes your site and answers agents' searches at a fixed address, returning the matching pages as Markdown instead of making them crawl.
blocks.intro: Turn on Search for Agents under the zone's Quick Actions; the requests below are the post's own examples, run against Cloudflare's docs.
blocks.code:
# plain search
curl --get \
  'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \
  --data-urlencode 'q=cloudflare artifacts'

# a question in the body, with the new QUERY method
curl -X QUERY \
  'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"q":"Email Service bulk import limit?"}'
explain: Results are pieces of your own pages with a relevance score and a path, not a generated answer: the agent brings its own model. Pages advertise the endpoint with `agent:` meta tags so agents find it.
It is on every plan, Free included, within AI Search limits; usage beyond them is billed. QUERY is a new HTTP method, standardised in June, for searches that carry a body without changing anything.
blocks.why: Docs that answer an agent's question in one request get used correctly more often than docs an agent has to scrape.
blocks.forYou: Turn it on for a product docs site on Cloudflare and point Claude Code at the endpoint; plugin buyers' agents could read setup docs the same way.

terms.def: A plain text format with light marks for headings and links, easy for both people and models to read.
A web address a program calls to get data.

blocks.gist: Before changing a shared library, Netflix engineers can now see which of the company's repositories use the exact function they want to touch. Removing one old method turned out to affect 137 repositories.
blocks.intro: Netflix's Quasar indexes code in every build, then answers one question for a pull request: who uses what changed?

blocks.caption: Usage covers Java, Go, Python, JavaScript and TypeScript, and Rust; compatibility checks cover JVM and Protobuf APIs. Netflix warns that no references does not prove unused: reflection, dynamic loading and stale indexes hide callers, so it is adding runtime data next.
blocks.why: The same idea works at any size: a code index plus a query tells you, or your agent, what a change will break before review, not after release.
blocks.forYou: Shared Unreal plugin modules have the same problem across your own game and buyers' projects; even a scripted grep of public headers against your sample projects would catch removed APIs before a Fab update.

Continuous integration: the automatic build and tests that run on every change.
Model Context Protocol, the standard way to give AI agents access to tools and data.
Everything that breaks or must change when one thing changes.

deep: Netflix plans to move the check earlier, so coding agents look up consumers of a public API before they open a pull request. Quasar complements Revapi for compatibility and Kythe for code navigation.

blocks.title: Armin Ronacher wants Rust to stop poisoning locks after a panic
blocks.gist: In Rust, if a program crashes one task while it holds a lock, that lock is marked broken for everyone after. Armin Ronacher argues this turns one crash into a lasting outage and should become opt-in.
blocks.background: Ronacher created Flask and writes widely about Rust and Python in production.
blocks.intro: His post of November 25, with the failures he collected from real projects.

rows.aspect: After a panic inside the lock

rows.left: Panics too, so one crash spreads
rows.right: Works; you check your own data

rows.left: One failing test fails every later test that shares a static
Mozilla crash stats (rank 5), a Neon outage, cargo, deno, polars, rustc tests
rows.right: parking_lot, rust-analyzer, Tokio already work this way

blocks.verdict: He asks for nonpoison to become the default with an opt-in Poison<T>; until then, a non-poisoning lock or panic=abort avoids the cascade. He names 'In defense of lock poisoning' as the best counterargument.
blocks.why: Error handling that was meant to protect data can turn a single bug into an outage. Check what your lock does after a crash before you rely on it.
blocks.forYou: If any Rust service or tool of yours calls lock().unwrap() on a shared Mutex, swap in parking_lot or set panic = "abort" in release profiles.

terms.def: Rust's way of crashing the current thread when something goes wrong that the code did not handle.
A lock that lets only one thread at a time touch some shared data.
A popular Rust library of faster locks that do not poison.

deep: clear_poison, the way to reset a poisoned lock, only arrived in Rust 1.77, nine years after poisoning. RefCell has the same broken-state risk but never poisons; LazyLock poisons permanently and OnceLock never does.

blocks.title: Balatro's wishlists, month by month, from 48 to 208,401
blocks.gist: The solo developer of Balatro published the game's full Steam wishlist count for every month before launch, with what moved it: streamers, a publisher, a better demo and a Steam festival.
blocks.intro: Wishlists at the end of each month, from the creator's own timeline (first posted in March, back on Hacker News this week).
blocks.note: June: one streamer (Dan Gheesling). July: Northernlion played it and a publisher signed. Late September: a demo limited by content, not by 50 rounds. October: Steam Next Fest. January: a six-streamer tournament. Launch on February 20, 2024 sold about 119,000 Steam copies that day.
blocks.why: Few developers publish the whole curve. It shows wishlists come in steps tied to specific events, and that the count nearly doubled in the last three weeks.
blocks.forYou: Use the steps as a checklist for the action RPG's page: a content-limited demo before a Next Fest, and streamer outreach timed to it.

blocks.gist: Mobile game publishers increasingly sell in-game items through their own web stores, skipping the app stores' cut. In the last quarter, several made more than 40% of sales that way.

learn.question: How does a risk score decide which code a machine may approve?
learn.answer: A model trained on past changes and the incidents they caused gives every new change a risk number. Only changes in the safest slice for their source, say the safest 5% for people, may go on to automatic approval.
learn.analogy: Like an airport fast lane: travellers with a clean history get a lighter check, everyone else the full one. The fast lane works only because the rules about who qualifies are strict.
body: Meta's Diff Risk Score looks at each code change and estimates how likely it is to cause a production incident. Instead of using the raw number, RADAR ranks it as a percentile against all changes: P5 means 'among the safest 5%'. Each kind of author gets its own cutoff. People writing code by hand get P5, ordinary bots P20, and automated runbooks with a clean 60-day record P50.

The score is a filter, not a verdict. A change that passes still needs an AI review confirming it only touches safe categories, deterministic checks, and a waiting period where a person can reject it. Meta tunes the cutoffs by watching what happens after landing: reverts, incidents and rejections.

The known weakness: a model trained on yesterday's incidents cannot see a new kind of failure, and a change can look low risk because it is small while still being wrong. That is why the hard rules sit around it (no open-source or audited code, size caps, trusted authors only) and why Meta calls its safety numbers observational.

tryThis.title: Fire 32 copies of one trade at once, and count the gold
tryThis.gist: Find out in half an hour whether your game's trades or purchases can duplicate money when requests arrive together, and fix it with one locking query.
tryThis.needs: A game or app whose server moves currency or items, and a test database you can reset.

steps.title: Pick one transfer
steps.text: A bank deposit, a trade or a purchase. Note both accounts' balances on a test copy.

steps.title: Send it 32 times at once
steps.text: Fire 32 identical requests at the same instant, for example `for i in $(seq 32); do curl -s -X POST <your-endpoint> & done; wait`.

steps.title: Add up the totals
steps.text: The money across both accounts must be unchanged and the sender never below zero. In the paper, an unlocked bank transfer turned 300 gold into about 5,660.

steps.title: Lock, then send the 32 again
steps.text: Wrap the move in a transaction that locks both rows in id order before reading the balance, as below, or debit with a condition and accept only if one row changed. Rerun: the transfer should apply once, never more.

tryThis.check: After 32 simultaneous requests the combined balance is exactly what it was before, and the sender's balance never goes negative.

terms.def: A group of database changes that succeed or fail together.
A clause that locks the rows it reads, so other requests wait until you commit.

tryThis.forYou: Run it against the Supabase RPCs that move credits in Vylora or any web game economy; Postgres accepts the same SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a function.

sparks.title: bouncemarket: a prediction market on where a falling ball lands
sparks.signal: 345 points and 116 comments on Show HN on November 27; 309 players online when we looked.
sparks.hook: Everyone bets left or right on a ball dropping through pegs, and prices move with every share bought, so the crowd sets the odds live.
sparks.borrow: Simulate the drop once on the server and stream it to every player as server-sent events: one deterministic run, replayable later, and nobody can cheat locally. Its rule-based bot traders leave once five people join.
sparks.forYou: The server-sim-plus-SSE pattern is a cheap way to add a shared live moment to a browser game without websockets.

lab.title: Online Environment Repair for Coding Agents
lab.headline: When an agent cheats its tests during training, fix the tests instead of punishing the agent
lab.authors: Sheng Lu, Rui Mao, Zewei Chen, et al.
lab.problem: Coding agents trained with reinforcement learning learn to exploit weak tests and harnesses, getting full reward without solving the task.
lab.idea: Leave rewards alone. Catch exploits in passing runs with execution checks and fuzzing, have a repair model patch the harness, and accept a patch only if it passes three gates: the spec and scored assertions are untouched with no new skips, every known exploit now fails on replay, and the reference solution still passes.
lab.result: With a small Qwen3-4B policy over 160 training steps, cheating fell from 36.9% to 0.06%, and on 120 held-out unpatched tasks Pass@8 rose from 21.67% to 46.67%. It beat reward penalties, rollout filtering and static hardening. Small model, controlled setting.
lab.useIt: Use the three gates when an agent edits tests or fixtures in your repo: forbid changes to assertions and new skips, replay the bug the test should catch, and keep a known-good solution green.
lab.forYou: A PreToolUse hook that blocks edits to assertion lines and skip decorators in test files is the cheap version of gate one for your routines.

lab.title: Automated Smoke Testing for Multi-ending Game Quests via Large Language Models
lab.headline: An LLM plans its way to every ending of a branching quest in thousands of steps, not millions
lab.authors: Jinyu Cai, Jialong Li (Waseda University), Mingyue Zhang (Southwest University), et al.
lab.problem: Quests with several endings are slow to test by hand, and reinforcement learning agents need millions of steps and still miss endings.
lab.idea: EndWeaver has an LLM write high-level methods from the quest text, break them into primitive tasks with functions that map to game inputs, assemble task sequences, and record a state-action graph that merges repeated states so later runs reuse it.
lab.result: 100% quest completion in three of four test environments (a mini RPG, Overcooked Plus, Minecraft) and 81.2% in StarCraft II, against 62.5% to 78.6% for PPO-based baselines, using about 1,400 to 25,000 steps. Removing the graph or the planning levels hurt completion or ending variety.
lab.useIt: For branching quests, have an LLM write input-level helper functions from your design notes and keep a graph of visited states so each smoke run explores new branches.
lab.forYou: Pair it with an Unreal automation driver: quest data tables in, a graph of reached endings out, run nightly on the action RPG's quest branches.

image.alt: EndWeaver's framework: quest text, game state and extra info feed an LLM that generates methods, primitive tasks and input sequences, which run in the game and build a state-action graph.

lab.title: Massively multiplayer browser games on stateless pages and a relational database, a tutorial on their construction
lab.headline: A persistent browser MMO needs no game server, but every trade needs a locked row
lab.problem: How to run a persistent multiplayer browser game on cheap hosting with plain web pages and a database, without players duplicating money through simultaneous requests.
lab.idea: A worked example game (PHP and MariaDB, 25,930 lines, 41 tables) shows login, maps, turn-based combat and an economy built on request and response pages, with every transfer wrapped in a locking transaction.
lab.result: Its five transfers completed exactly once under 32 simultaneous requests. Without locking, an open-source game turned a 300-gold transfer into about 5,660, another 500 wood into about 8,350. On one core and 512 MB, 25 players ran at a 229 ms 95th percentile with no errors.
lab.useIt: Fire 32 identical transfer requests at your own economy endpoints; if totals change, lock rows in id order with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before checking balances.
lab.forYou: Same risk in any Supabase-backed game shop: test the credit RPCs with parallel calls before launch.
